Content:
Recall that the biconditional statement [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q] is true if and only if [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] have the same truth value.

Content:
The relation "[MATH: \Leftrightarrow]" between two statements is an equivalence relation because it's reflexive, symmetric, and transitive:

Content:
- [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow P] is always true because [MATH: P] has the same truth value as itself.
- If [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q] is true, then [MATH: Q\Leftrightarrow P] is also true. If [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] have the same truth value, then [MATH: Q] and [MATH: P] also have the same truth value.
- If [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q] and [MATH: Q\Leftrightarrow R] are both true, then [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow R] is also true.

Content:
Suppose have the following chain of equivalent statements:

Content:
[MATH: P \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad Q \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad R]

Content:
There are only two ways in which this chain of equivalences is true:

Content:
- [MATH: P,Q,] and [MATH: R] are all true
- [MATH: P,Q,] and [MATH: R] are all false

Content:
Consider the following predicate for [MATH: x\in\mathbb Z.]

Content:
[MATH: P(x): \quad 2x-3 = 5]

Content:
This is equivalent to the statement [MATH: x=4,] and this can be proved using a chain of equivalent statements as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 2x − 3 = 5_(⏟)_(P(x))⇔2x = 8_(⏟)_(Q(x))⇔x = 4_(⏟)_(R(x))]

Content:
Note that substituting [MATH: {\color{blue}{x}}={\color{blue}{4}}] into [MATH: P,Q,] and [MATH: R] gives a truth value of "true" [MATH: (\textrm{T})] in each case:

Content:
[MATH: 2 ⋅ 4 − 3 = 5_(⏟)_(T)⇔2 ⋅ 4 = 8_(⏟)_(T)⇔4 = 4_(⏟)_(T)]

Content:
However, substituting [MATH: {\color{red}{x}}={\color{red}{3}}] into [MATH: P,Q,] and [MATH: R] gives a truth value of "false" [MATH: (\textrm{F})] in each case:

Content:
[MATH: 2 ⋅ 3 − 3 = 5_(⏟)_(F)⇔2 ⋅ 3 = 8_(⏟)_(F)⇔3 = 4_(⏟)_(F)]

Content:
In general, we can prove a biconditional [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q] by finding a set of statements [MATH: R_1, R_2, \ldots, R_n] and using them to form a chain of equivalent statements connecting [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q{:}]

Content:
[MATH: P \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad R_1 \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad R_2 \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad \cdots \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad R_n \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad Q]

Content:
In fact, you've been implicitly using this type of argument throughout your mathematical career! Solving linear equations is just one example.

Content:

> [MATH: 15∣n]

> Case [MATH: \Leftarrow{:}] We need to show that
